summary: I classified all 209 committed events in the 11 final_v6 runs by hand and compared them against the 77 events of artifacts/baseline_main, then traced every attempt, world judgment and continuity verdict in the ledgers. The change did the thing it set out to do: the notification bookkeeping that made baseline group_coordination unreadable (40+ of 56 events are 'X's phone buzzes, but they do not look at it') is genuinely gone, the structural attention check refused 58 attempts to answer attention with something other than attention, individual people are often excellently evidence-grounded (Dev pulls out citing his clutch repair, Nina defers over her mother then commits after speaking to her, Marian keeps a paper diary and crosses bookings out in it, Tomas holds out two days because he hates hosting and then volunteers anyway), and I found no stereotyping - 81-year-old Ethel does the pairing herself. But two defect classes now dominate that the deleted event-quality reviewer was the only check on, and they are worse than the machinery it replaced. 91 of 209 committed events (44%, not the reported 14%) are a restatement that nothing changed, a device micro-step, a near-duplicate of an act already committed, or a flat contradiction of committed state; the deterministic dedupe caught 11 word-for-word repeats while ~46 near-duplicates survived, including the decisive act of holiday_deposit committed twice. Worst: in holiday_deposit the actor's conditional intention 'If confirmed, transfer 400 to Marian' was executed unconditionally and 30 seconds BEFORE the check it was conditioned on, that check said the money had not arrived, and the 400 pounds - two thirds of the scenario's entire question - was then never resolved by anything, so the run's own judge returned YES at 09-16T08:42 and UNRESOLVED at 09-16T22:26 on the same event record. The old failure ('the decisive act was destroyed and its absence became the answer') has not been fixed, it has been relocated.

findings.title: Conditional intentions are executed unconditionally and out of order; 400 pounds of the deposit is committed on a condition the runtime then denies, never resolved, and the judge flips YES to UNRESOLVED on the same record
findings.evidence: artifacts/final_v6/holiday_deposit ledger seq 506 (actor_call c206, intentions '.0 Check my bank account to confirm Nina's 200 transfer has arrived' / '.1 If confirmed, transfer 400 to Marian Prowse's account'), e519 att=ac206.1 @2026-09-14T15:57:43, e522 att=ac206.0 @15:58:13 ('Nina's 200 transfer has not yet arrived'), world judgment seq 528 ('she is waiting for Nina's 200 to arrive before sending the deposit, but she has already sent the transfer'), terminal_check c574 seq 1287 = YES ('Ruth initiated a 400 transfer to Marian (e519) ... totaling 600 deposited') vs seq 1385 = UNRESOLVED ('No deposit of 600 has been deposited'); same pattern at ac570.0/.1 (e1290 @08:42:13 before e1293 @08:42:43) and ac437.0/.1; dispatch at sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:516-525
findings.why_it_matters: The intentions of one turn are dispatched as independent world_steps and then fire from a time-ordered queue, so sibling .1 can land before sibling .0 and the 'If confirmed' prefix is stripped: Ruth sends 400 pounds she has not got, on a condition that is false, half a minute before checking it. No later event has the 400 arrive, bounce, or reach Marian - she checks her balance at e1321 and only looks for the Leeds 600 - so two thirds of the scenario's answer is a dangling thread. The judge reads the same journal as YES once and UNRESOLVED four times. This is the merged-main chain in new clothes: the decisive act is destroyed by the machinery and its absence becomes the answer.
findings.suggested_fix: Adjudicate a turn's intentions as an ordered dependent sequence - each world_step sees the events its predecessors committed, and an intention whose stated condition was not satisfied by the predecessor's committed outcome is dropped rather than fired.

findings.title: All five OVERRULED continuity verdicts are correct diagnoses of contradictions that were then committed, and the code keeps the failed correction while the comment claims the original stands
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:438-488 (comment at 463-467 says 'the ORIGINAL reply stands'; the loop breaks with `parsed` from attempt 1, the corrected reply, and attempt 0's reply is discarded). anti_stereotype ledger seq 103-105 ('the support representative is already on the line asking her to hold, which directly negates her belief that the line does not open until Thursday') then seq 106/111-120 committing e120 'Ethel waits on hold while the representative looks up her account' at 2026-09-10T07:00, 22h59m after the hold began at e101 2026-09-09T08:01. feedback_deadline seq 334-336 ('Aline already finished reading and sent comments at 13:34, so proposing to continue reading contradicts what has already occurred') then e333. lease_return seq 36-38, group_coordination seq 500-502, evidence_avoiding seq 65-67
findings.why_it_matters: 5 for 5: every time the one surviving reviewer objected twice, it was right, and the runtime committed the contradiction anyway. Two of the five became committed world events that cannot happen - a 23-hour hold on a support call in which both parties stay on the line, and a supervisor still reading a chapter she has already finished and emailed. Worse, the retained reply is the second one, produced under an instruction that named the contradiction: it is the more distorted of the two, not the person's own words. The branch traded 'a read-only check can silence somebody' for 'a read-only check that is right cannot stop anything', which is not the only pair of options.
findings.suggested_fix: On a second failure, do not commit the reply verbatim - send the objection to the world as the trigger ('this person believes X, the record shows Y') and let the world adjudicate the mismatch, so the contradiction is resolved in the world rather than recorded in it.

findings.title: Near-duplicate re-commitment of the same act is the corpus's dominant defect; the exact-string dedupe catches 11 and misses ~46, including the decisive act committed twice
findings.evidence: world_mind.py:235-244 (dedupe is `contained(description).casefold() in already_committed`, i.e. word-for-word only; 11 drops across all 11 runs). Survivors: holiday_deposit e789 and e819 both 'Ruth calls Marian Prowse and [says/tells her] the deposit won't be coming, so they will have to release Cove Cottage' (12:00 and 12:01) - the decisive act twice; e804/e863 hearing it twice; e873/e884 the same release text to Nina twice, later observed as 'the two text messages from Ruth' (e1095), so the duplicate became world state; Marian calls the Leeds couple five times (e891, e902, e916, e930, e939) after they already answered at e919; six identical 'Nina's 200 has still not arrived' checks (e522, e543, e562, e646, e765, e795). anti_stereotype: the rep looks up the same account three times (e145, e179, e191), Ethel enters the pairing code three times (e234, e242, e261). feedback_deadline: e58/e68 same minute, e153/e162 same minute, e170/e179 same minute, e275/e288/e304. lease_return: the lease is signed in e61, e65 and e81
findings.why_it_matters: By my hand count 46 of 209 committed events (22%) are the same act again under different words. This is exactly the work the brief says moved to `make_world_validator`, and the deterministic version cannot do it: a model never writes the same sentence twice. It is not cosmetic - a duplicated release call and a duplicated text are read back by later events as two separate real acts, and in holiday_deposit the duplicate release is what the person on the other end responds to.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the dedupe a semantic key instead of the raw string (verb + object + actor, or an embedding threshold) and refuse an event that repeats an act already committed by the same actor within the same span.

findings.title: evaluation/interface_mechanics.py does not measure what the 52%-to-14% headline claims: 11 of its 30 hits are named people acting, three of them the very acts the terminal answers cite
findings.evidence: evaluation/interface_mechanics.py:32-50. NO_CHANGE matches bare `\bsits?\b`, so 'Aline sits at her desk, opens the thesis chapter PDF ... resuming reading' (feedback_deadline e162, e275) is scored as 'a restatement that nothing has changed'; it matches `are still` inside dialogue ('asks if they are still interested', holiday_deposit e927). SUBJECT_IS_A_DEVICE is not anchored to the subject, so 'document, saves' and 'document and scans' match: lease_return e90 'Aisha scans the signed lease document, saves the PDF, composes an email to Tomas Herrera ... and sends the email' is counted as a device acting on its own, and e90 is the event the YES cites. Same for anti_stereotype e324 (cited by that run's YES) via 'the terminal shows', evidence_avoiding e44 (Dana sending a follow-up) via a trailing clause, and holiday_deposit e873/e884 via the quoted message body 'your transfer hadn't arrived'. Conversely it misses every near-duplicate, every 'X hears/sees Y' event, all four holiday_deposit starting events, and group_coordination e110/e364/e402/e408 ('does not check', 'without checking' are not in the pattern)
findings.why_it_matters: The implementer has already had to correct this metric once for under-reporting by 5x, and it is still not a usable proxy for 'how human does this trajectory look'. My hand classification of the same 209 events gives 91 (44%) that are non-events, device micro-steps, near-duplicates or self-contradictions - per run: anti_stereotype 17/26, feedback_deadline 16/31, lease_return 7/10, holiday_deposit 32/91. The tool's own category, re-scored by me, is roughly 40 not 30, with 11 false positives and ~20 misses. Publishing 'machinery 52% -> 14%' as the evidence that the trajectories became more human is an overclaim of the same kind the report was written to retire.
findings.suggested_fix: Anchor SUBJECT_IS_A_DEVICE to the sentence subject, strip quoted message bodies before matching, delete the bare `sits?`/`are still` alternatives, and add near-duplicate and reciprocal-observation counts as separate reported columns.

findings.title: Committed events carry no duration, so actors are routinely in two places at once and nothing can detect it
findings.evidence: journal.jsonl schema across all 11 runs has only `t` (no duration field; verified over all 209 events). feedback_deadline: e115 'Aline attends the hiring committee meeting from 08:31 to about 10:30' vs e123 @09:01 'continues reading the thesis chapter and typing comments for 30 minutes'; e214 @11:46 'teaches her 11:30 class' + e226 'continues teaching ... until it ends at 12:30' vs e217 @12:01 'reads the thesis chapter and types comments for about 90 minutes'; e186 @11:16 'saves her place ... to prepare for her 11:30 class' vs e170/e179 @11:16 'reads ... for about 45 minutes'; e259 @13:02 'about two-thirds of the way through' vs e296 @13:16 'making progress through the middle section'; e267 @13:03 'walks back to her office after teaching' though she has been at her desk since e234 @12:32. anti_stereotype e101 -> e120 (22h59m on hold). holiday_deposit e1074 @14:13 'Marian's phone rings with Ruth's call, but she is already on the phone with the Leeds couple and does not answer it' though she answered that call at e1055 @14:05 and the Leeds call ended at e966 @12:08. Only sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/envelope.py:107-142 bounds anything, and it bounds `after` (the scheduling delay, MAX_STEP_DAYS=30), never a described duration
findings.why_it_matters: The brief lists 'impossible durations' as legitimate reviewer work now handled deterministically. It is not: the only duration the code understands is how long until an event fires. An event that says it takes 90 minutes occupies zero simulated time, so the world can and does put the same person in a lecture theatre and at her desk in the same minute, and can leave a woman on hold for a day. Five of feedback_deadline's 31 events are physically impossible; that run's YES is built on a record that contradicts itself.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a code-owned `lasts` on the event envelope, advance that actor's own clock by it, and refuse any proposed event for an actor whose interval overlaps one already committed.

findings.title: Actors are consulted dozens of times and never do anything; one is woken 55 times over 14 simulated days for 185 model calls and 2 events
findings.evidence: artifacts/final_v6/cold_email: mark_cuban gets 55 consecutive actor turns, every one with zero intentions (actor_exchanges.jsonl + ledger semantic.actor_call), driven by 54 successive world_process `pending_progression` wakes whose reasons are paraphrases of each other ('Check if Mark Cuban has had a chance to look at his email inbox' twice verbatim, grounded_wakes.jsonl), then terminates incomplete_empty_queue at 2026-08-10T10:00:30 with cutoff 14:00:00. Corpus-wide 253 of 421 actor turns (60%) return no intentions: group_coordination tomas 35 of 46 and bea 12 of 15, holiday_deposit ruth 36 of 75 and nina 30 of 48 and marian 17 of 29, evidence_avoiding marcus_bell 4 of 4
findings.why_it_matters: The merged corpus's 19-identical-turn actor was called out as a defect; this corpus contains a 55-turn one. It is better in aggregate than baseline_main (60% vs 86% empty turns) but the worst single case is worse in absolute terms, because the same scenario now runs three times as long to reach a weaker answer: baseline cold_email produced NO_AT_CUTOFF in 87 calls, final_v6 produces UNRESOLVED in 185. Fifty-five consecutive refusals to act ARE the answer to 'is this cold email likely to get a response'; spending them and then declining to answer because the queue emptied 3.5 hours early is the empty-queue failure relabelled, not removed.
findings.suggested_fix: Stop re-waking an actor on a `pending_progression` reason materially identical to the last one that produced nothing, and treat a long unbroken run of no-op turns as evidence bearing on the question rather than as a reason to keep polling.

findings.title: 32% of attempts vanish with no committed event, and the world's judgment often narrates the act as about to happen - so the world decides a person's choice in a way the new `by` identity guard cannot see
findings.evidence: 57 of 179 attempts across the 11 runs produce no journal event. negotiation ac22.0 'I reply to Priya confirming the sale at 1200 and ask when she'd like to pick up the kiln' -> world c24 'Dmitri has just seen Priya's acceptance and intends to reply immediately. He types a confirmation message' -> no event, and the run still resolves YES on an agreement the seller never confirmed. lease_return ac31.0 -> c33 'She is about to compose and send the email' -> no event. holiday_deposit ac174.2 'Transfer my own 200 deposit plus Nina's to Marian's account by Wednesday's deadline' -> c178, in which the world reasons about which option Ruth would pick ('she could pay both ... or wait ... Since Ruth is not keen on covering others again, she is lik...') -> no event. 53 of 459 world judgments (12%) narrate an unrealised intention. structural_refusals.jsonl records 58 refusals, all `attention_answer_without_attention`, and 0 `by`-identity refusals in any run
findings.why_it_matters: The branch's guarantee is that if the world declares `by` as someone other than the actor being adjudicated, control routes to that person and nothing is committed. That guard only exists when an event IS proposed. The world's other route to taking a decision away from a person - declining to commit their attempt while narrating it as imminent - is unguarded and fired 57 times, twice on the act a scenario turns on. 'Whose choice it is, is identity' is enforced against the loud version of the problem and not the quiet one.
findings.suggested_fix: Require every adjudicated attempt to return either an event or an explicit refusal with a cited obstacle, and count silent non-commits as a run-level defect in the metrics.

findings.title: The follow_up chain was deleted but delivery-as-event was not: reciprocal 'X hears/sees what Y just said' is still committed as ordinary events
findings.evidence: anti_stereotype e83, e86 (the rep hears the same explanation twice), e101, e160, e285 ('hears the terminal's audible beep or Ethel's voice' - the world hedging on which); holiday_deposit e804 and e863 (Marian hears the same sentence twice), e1044 ('Marian hears her phone ringing and sees Ruth's name on the caller ID'), e1061; evidence_responsive e21; group_coordination e36, e234 (a group-chat message that takes an hour to become 'posted'). All carry observed=True with observed_by already populated
findings.why_it_matters: The redesign's stated principle is that who a thing reached is `for`, whether they saw it is `observed_by`, and the attention question may only be answered with attention. These events answer it a third way - by committing the reception as a world change - which is the same bookkeeping the deleted follow_up/event_consequence chain produced, now indistinguishable from a real act. In anti_stereotype nine of 26 events are of this kind, which is why that run reads as a transcript of a call rather than a slice of a day.
findings.suggested_fix: Refuse an event whose description adds nothing beyond an actor perceiving an already-committed event, and record it as an observed_by update instead.

findings.title: World events contradict authoritative actor evidence and nothing checks them, because the surviving reviewer only reads actor replies
findings.evidence: evidence_avoiding: Marcus's private_context is 'He is on leave with his phone off until the following Tuesday (2026-09-08)', yet e44 at 2026-09-09T08:00 (Wednesday) commits 'the message ... is not yet delivered' because 'Marcus's phone is off'; the run then ends UNRESOLVED with 'No committed event shows Marcus Bell actually sending a reply'. The continuity reviewer at trajectory.py:527-546 sees only `rendered` (the actor's own view) and that actor's reply - never a proposed world event - and its own OVERRULED at seq 67 notes the leave had ended
findings.why_it_matters: With the event reviewer gone there is no check of any kind on whether a committed world fact is consistent with the evidence the scene declared. Here the world invented two extra days of a phone being off, which pre-determines the scenario's whole question: the test of whether an avoidant person replies is replaced by a test of whether an unreachable person replies, and the answer is manufactured rather than observed.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the world validator the scene's declared actor evidence and refuse an event that asserts a state the evidence dates as over.

findings.title: Starting events are committed as journal events although they are backstory, not changes, and one is internally dated against its own scene
findings.evidence: holiday_deposit e15-e18 ('Ruth ... is aware that ... has not yet paid ... is waiting to see how the group will handle it'; 'Dev ... has expressed enthusiasm ... but has not yet paid'; 'Nina ... has not replied ... has not communicated her decision'; 'Marian ... has not yet received any deposit'); lease_return e11, lease_other_names e11, negotiation e11 ('No agreement has been reached yet'); anti_stereotype e11 'The simulation starts at the opening of the vendor's support line on Thursday' at 2026-09-09T07:00 while that scene's shared_context says the line opens Thursday 2026-09-10
findings.why_it_matters: Eight of 209 events are statements that nothing has happened, which is the category both the world prompt and the removed reviewer named as forbidden, seeded by the compiler and never questioned. The anti_stereotype one is worse than untidy: it opens the support line a day early, which is why Ethel's own turns keep saying 'the line doesn't open until Thursday 8am' while she is mid-call, and why the run needs a 23-hour hold to stay coherent. e11 also breaks the fourth wall by naming 'the simulation' inside a committed world event.
findings.suggested_fix: Seed opening state as facts and private context rather than journal events, and validate that a starting event's time is consistent with the times its own shared_context asserts.

findings.title: plumber_confirm's decisive act is addressed to nobody and the run resolves YES on it
findings.evidence: artifacts/final_v6/plumber_confirm e20 'Sam Okonjo picks up his phone and sends a reply to Bristol Plumbing's text message confirming the Thursday 8am slot' with for=[] and observed=false; initial_actor_states.json lists one actor, sam_okonjo, so Bristol Plumbing cannot be an audience. Baseline's e20 for the same scenario at least quotes the reply text
findings.why_it_matters: The run's YES rests on a message the record shows reached no one, in a scenario whose whole content is whether a confirmation reaches the plumber. It is a two-event trajectory, so this is small, but it is the cleanest instance of `for` being empty because the counterparty was never modelled - the answer is about a delivery the world cannot represent.
findings.suggested_fix: Compile any named counterparty a scenario's question depends on as an actor, or record off-stage recipients explicitly so `for` is never empty on a delivery-bearing act.
